title: Abu Simbel’s giant temples were sawn into over 1,000 blocks and moved uphill

cover.alt: Two of the colossal seated statues of Ramesses II on the sandstone facade of the Great Temple at Abu Simbel, seen from below against a deep blue sky.

body: Ramesses II had two temples carved into a sandstone cliff beside the Nile in the 13th century BC. In the 1960s the new Aswan High Dam was about to raise the river behind it into Lake Nasser, which would have drowned them, so UNESCO led an international campaign to save them. Engineers sawed the temples into **more than 1,000 blocks**, the smallest weighing about seven tons, and rebuilt them 208 m further inland and 65 m higher. The work ran from 1964 to 1968, and an artificial hill now stands in for the original cliff behind them.

slides.question: How much higher was the Great Temple rebuilt than where Ramesses II carved it?
slides.explanation: About 65 m higher, and 208 m further inland. The Small Temple of Nefertari went up about 67 m.

slides.alt: A scale model at the Nubian Museum in Aswan showing the riverbank site where the Abu Simbel temples were first carved and the higher ground they were moved to.
slides.caption: A model in the Nubian Museum, Aswan, shows the temples’ original riverside site, now under Lake Nasser, and the higher ground where they stand today.

steps.label: Inject resin to strengthen the sandstone
Saw it into blocks along 6 mm cuts
Code each block and truck it on sand
Cover the back with an artificial hill

events.text: Explorer Johann Burckhardt sees the Great Temple’s top in the sand
Explorer Giovanni Belzoni clears sand for 22 days and walks in
The first block is lifted out on 21 May
The rebuilt temples are inaugurated on 22 September

slides.label: height of each of the four seated statues of Ramesses II on the Great Temple’s facade
slides.text: The facade is about 33 m high and 38 m wide. The statues of the king and queen on the Small Temple are slightly more than 10 m tall.

slides.question: One colossus lost its head and torso in an ancient earthquake. What did the engineers do with them?
slides.explanation: The fallen pieces were not reattached. They were placed at the statue’s feet in the same positions they had been lying in before the move.
